name: Angkor Wat
scope: The largest religious monument on Earth, a 12th-century temple-city in the Cambodian jungle covering ~400 acres (162 ha). T1: its five stone towers are built to model a sacred mountain from Hindu myth, the home of the gods (invert the wonder: 'the world's biggest temple is a map of the cosmos' is the hook; answer = Mount Meru). T1 bonus: it is the only building pictured on any national flag (answer = Cambodia's flag). T2: the wide moat ringing the temple isn't just defense -- on the cosmic map it stands for the primordial ocean at the world's rim (answer = the cosmic ocean). T2/T3: nearly every Khmer temple faces the sunrise, but Angkor Wat faces the OPPOSITE way, which scholars tie to the god Vishnu and to death (answer = it faces west). T3: a 49-metre carved gallery shows gods and demons hauling a giant serpent to churn the sea for the elixir of immortality (answer = the Churning of the Ocean of Milk). T3: unlike its jungle-swallowed neighbours, Angkor Wat was never truly abandoned -- one community kept worshipping here, which is why it survived intact (answer = Buddhist monks). T4: it began as a shrine to the Hindu god Vishnu, then Cambodia's changing faith reconsecrated it to the religion it still serves (answer = Buddhism). T4: its 5-10 million sandstone blocks were floated ~50 km from one quarry-mountain by canal (answer = Phnom Kulen / Mount Kulen). T5: airborne laser scanning finally mapped 'greater Angkor' beneath the forest as one of the largest pre-industrial cities on Earth, ~1,000 sq km (answer = LIDAR). T5: the whole city ran on giant reservoirs called barays, a water grid whose failure in drought helped doom Angkor (answer = the barays / West Baray).
source: Grokipedia (checked first per source priority; returned 403 at fetch time); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat (Guinness 'largest religious structure' 162.6 ha, Suryavarman II 1122-1150, Vishnu->Buddhist, five towers=Mount Meru / moat=cosmic ocean, west-facing, 49 m Churning-of-the-Ocean-of-Milk relief, Phnom Kulen sandstone ~40-50 km, LIDAR-revealed greater Angkor + barays, on Cambodia's flag).
framing_note: Scene-led place ladder: every stem names Angkor Wat and the scene; the player must KNOW the wonder (Mount Meru, the west orientation, the Churning relief), never deduce it from a stem clause. Invert the wonder on T1 -- lead with 'the world's largest temple' as HOOK, make Mount Meru the answer. Distractors = other real Angkor/Khmer features and other world temples so all four stay live. Respect the Hindu-Buddhist cosmology as genuine sacred meaning, no smug secular gloss. Dinner-test payoff = the LIDAR-revealed hidden mega-city (T5) and the only-building-on-a-flag gem.
history_overlap: Suryavarman II's reign, the Khmer Empire's rise, and the 15th-century abandonment/relocation to Phnom Penh are history-bank episodes -- keep every answer a place-wonder (towers, moat, orientation, relief, sandstone source, LIDAR extent, barays), not a dynasty timeline.

name: Angkor Thom & the Bayon
scope: The last great walled capital of the Khmer Empire, raised by Jayavarman VII, with the Bayon temple at its exact center. T2: from the Bayon's towers, more than 200 giant serene stone FACES gaze out in every direction, each wearing the same faint smile (answer = the smiling stone faces of the Bayon). T3: those faces are read two ways at once -- as a Buddhist bodhisattva of compassion AND as the god-king himself (answer = Avalokiteshvara). T3: you enter the 9-square-km city through monumental gate-towers each crowned with four more of those outward-gazing faces (answer = the face-towers / gopura gates). T4: the Bayon's lower galleries carve not gods but ORDINARY LIFE -- a market, a cockfight, a woman giving birth, a naval battle on the Tonle Sap (answer = everyday life of the Khmer). T4/T5: Jayavarman VII switched the empire's state religion, which is why his capital's temple is Buddhist where Angkor Wat began Hindu (answer = Mahayana Buddhism). T5: a causeway into the city is lined with rows of stone giants gripping a serpent -- the Churning of the Ocean of Milk rebuilt as a bridge (answer = the gods-and-demons causeway).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayon (~200 large faces, ~54 towers originally / 37 standing, Jayavarman VII late 12th-early 13th c, Avalokiteshvara-and/or-king dual reading, everyday-life bas-reliefs, Mahayana Buddhist state temple); Angkor Thom layout (9 sq km walled city, face-gates, causeway) from established domain knowledge.
framing_note: Place ladder anchored on the Bayon/Angkor Thom; the serene many-faced towers are the T2 hook and dinner-test image. Scene-led, no 'what is the Bayon?' definition shell. Label the faces' identity as scholarly READING (bodhisattva AND king) rather than settled fact -- accuracy rail. Distractors = other Angkor temples and other Buddhist/Hindu iconography, all real. Keep answers to the site's carvings and layout.
history_overlap: Jayavarman VII's reign and the empire's political peak belong to history; keep answers to the faces, gates, everyday-life reliefs, and the causeway.

name: Ta Prohm
scope: The Angkor temple the jungle never let go. T2: while other Angkor temples were cleared and rebuilt, restorers deliberately LEFT this one in the grip of the forest exactly as they found it (answer = it was left unrestored on purpose). T3: enormous pale roots pour over its walls and prise the stone blocks apart -- mostly one huge species that towers above the ruin (answer = the silk-cotton tree, Tetrameles nudiflora, alongside strangler figs). T4: a surviving temple inscription records the staggering workforce it took to run this one monastery -- nearly 80,000 people including 615 dancers (answer = ~80,000 attendants). Bonus: it became the world's most famous 'lost temple' after a 2001 film shot here (answer = Tomb Raider).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm (Jayavarman VII late 12th-early 13th c, originally Rajavihara, deliberately left picturesque/unrestored, Tetrameles nudiflora silk-cotton + strangler fig, ~80,000 attendants incl. 615 dancers, Tomb Raider 2001).
framing_note: Tight gem ladder; the strangler-root grip is the whole draw and the dinner-test image. Name the actual dominant tree species (accuracy rail -- it's mostly the silk-cotton tree, NOT just 'a fig'). Distractors = other Angkor temples and other rainforest trees, all real. LANE: the trees are scenery for a PLACE fact (roots wrecking stonework) -- do NOT drift into tree biology (that's the animal/plant lane); keep the answer the temple-in-the-forest.
history_overlap: None significant -- the workforce inscription is a place-fact of the site, not a distinct history episode.

name: Borobudur
scope: The largest Buddhist monument on Earth, a 9th-century stone mountain on Java you climb like a pilgrim. T1: seen from above, the whole monument forms one giant geometric diagram of the Buddhist universe -- a shape you walk (answer = a mandala). T1/T2: you don't go INSIDE Borobudur; you spiral UP its terraces from base to summit, and the climb itself is the journey through the cosmos (answer = you climb it / it's a walked pilgrimage). T2: ringing the top terraces sit 72 bell-shaped stone cages, each hiding a Buddha you can just glimpse through the stone lattice (answer = the 72 perforated stupas). T3: along the galleries runs the world's most complete set of Buddhist story-carvings -- 2,672 relief panels tracing the Buddha's path (answer = the 2,672 relief panels / largest Buddhist relief series). T3: the three stacked levels have names -- the world of desire at the base, of form above, of formlessness at the crown (answer = Kamadhatu / Rupadhatu / Arupadhatu). T4: built by the Sailendra dynasty ~825 CE, then lost for centuries under jungle and volcanic ash (answer = buried under ash and jungle). T4: it stands in one of the most volcano-dense regions on Earth, in view of one of the world's most active volcanoes (answer = Mount Merapi). T5: a 1970s-80s UNESCO rescue took the monument APART -- over a million blocks numbered, cleaned, and rebuilt on a new hidden foundation (answer = dismantled and reassembled stone by stone).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur (world's largest Buddhist temple, 2,672 relief panels, 504 Buddha statues, 72 perforated stupas, Sailendra ~9th c / ~825 CE, giant mandala, three cosmological levels Kamadhatu/Rupadhatu/Arupadhatu, abandoned under volcanic ash + jungle, Raffles 1814, 1975-82 dismantle-and-rebuild with >1 million stones).
framing_note: Place ladder; the mandala-you-climb is the controlling image, the 72 latticed stupas the dinner-test payoff. Scene-led -- never 'what is the largest Buddhist temple?'. Teach 'mandala' before testing it (§16 teach-before-test). Distractors = Prambanan, Bagan, other stupas, other cosmology terms, all real. Respect the pilgrimage meaning on its own terms. LANE: Merapi is the geographic/volcano anchor (the earth-process the place sits in) -- keep the answer the volcano's name/place-fact, light touch, not volcanology mechanics.
history_overlap: The Sailendra dynasty's politics belong to history; keep answers to the structure, cosmology, burial, and restoration. Raffles' 1814 rediscovery can surface here as a place-fact, but the colonial-administration story leans history.

name: Prambanan
scope: The soaring Hindu answer to Borobudur, a few miles away on the same Javanese plain. T2: where Borobudur is a low broad mandala, Prambanan spikes UPWARD -- its central tower stabs 47 m into the sky, the tallest Hindu temple in Indonesia (answer = the 47-metre central Shiva tower). T3: its three main towers honor the Hindu trinity, and the biggest belongs to the destroyer-god (answer = Shiva / the Trimurti). T4: carved along the inner balustrades, panel after panel, runs one great Indian epic of a prince, a stolen wife, and a monkey army (answer = the Ramayana). Bonus: local legend says a jilted spirit-summoner built '1,000 temples' here overnight and turned a princess to stone (answer = the Roro Jonggrang legend -- flag as folklore).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prambanan (9th c ~850 CE, Mataram Kingdom, dedicated to the Trimurti, 47 m central Shiva temple, largest Hindu temple site in Indonesia / 2nd-largest in SE Asia, Ramayana bas-reliefs, originally 240 temples, Roro Jonggrang / 1,000-temple legend).
framing_note: Short ladder that plays off Borobudur (up-spiking Hindu vs broad Buddhist) -- a deliberate contrast pair; a nearby-sister distractor keeps it live. Scene-led. Accuracy rail: label the Roro Jonggrang tale explicitly as legend. Distractors = Borobudur, Angkor, Indian temples, the other Trimurti gods. Keep answers to place/architecture facts.

name: Bagan
scope: A plain in Myanmar where, at dawn, hot-air balloons drift over thousands of brick spires poking out of the mist along the Irrawaddy. T1: this ~40-square-mile plain is studded with temples and pagodas -- not dozens but THOUSANDS (invert the wonder: the balloon-at-dawn scene is the hook; answer = over 2,000 surviving temples). T2: at its 11th-13th-century height as the Pagan Kingdom's capital, the count was even more staggering before time and quakes thinned it (answer = more than 10,000 originally). T3: the whitewashed, gilded Ananda is the plain's most beloved temple, its dim corridors lit to reveal towering standing Buddhas (answer = the Ananda Temple). T3: the massive, brooding Dhammayangyi is the LARGEST temple on the plain, its inner sanctums mysteriously bricked up (answer = Dhammayangyi). T4: the plain sits in an active seismic zone -- a 2016 earthquake damaged nearly 400 monuments in a single day (answer = the 2016 earthquake). T5: nearly every structure here is BRICK, not carved stone like Angkor or Borobudur -- which is why Bagan reads as a forest of red-brown spires (answer = it is built of brick).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagan (Pagan Kingdom capital 9th-13th c, >10,000 temples originally / >2,200 surviving, Ananda ~1105, Dhammayangyi largest 1167-70, 2016 earthquake damaged ~400 monuments, 104 sq km on the Irrawaddy).
framing_note: Place ladder; the sea-of-thousands-of-spires-at-dawn is the T1 hook and dinner-test image. Invert the wonder -- lead with the balloon-at-dawn scene, make the count and the named temples the answers, never 'what is the largest temple city?'. Distractors = Angkor, Borobudur, other temple-cities, other named Bagan temples. The 2016 quake is the earth-process anchor; keep answers place-facts.
history_overlap: Pagan Kingdom political history and its fall to the Mongols belong to history; keep answers to the plain, the named temples, the brick, and the quake.

name: Sigiriya
scope: A sheer rock tower jutting 180 m straight out of the Sri Lankan jungle, with a palace on top. T1: a 5th-century king built his royal palace not on a hill but on the FLAT SUMMIT of this 180-metre rock column (answer = on top of the rock). T2: the only way up once passed THROUGH a giant brick lion -- you climbed the staircase between its paws and into its open mouth, which named the rock 'Lion Rock' (answer = the Lion Gate / Sinhagiri). T3: sheltered in a rock pocket halfway up survive vivid painted 'cloud maidens,' among the oldest surviving frescoes in Sri Lanka (answer = the Sigiriya frescoes / damsels). T3: below them runs a wall once polished so glassy the king could see his own reflection walking past (answer = the Mirror Wall). T4: that Mirror Wall is now covered in over a thousand poems scratched by visitors 1,200+ years ago -- ancient graffiti admiring the maidens (answer = ancient graffiti / poems). T4/T5: King Kashyapa built this fortress-capital partly out of fear, having seized the throne from his father -- then lost his last battle at its foot (answer = King Kashyapa). T5: at the rock's base spread symmetrical water gardens whose fountains STILL spurt in the rainy season, among the oldest landscaped gardens on Earth (answer = the water gardens / working fountains).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya (~180 m granite inselberg, King Kashyapa 477-495 CE, Lion Gate / Sinhagiri, cloud-maiden frescoes, Mirror Wall with 1,500+ poems from the 8th-10th c, ancient water gardens with fountains that still work in the wet season).
framing_note: Place ladder; the climb-through-a-lion's-mouth to a palace in the sky is the controlling image and dinner-test payoff. Scene-led. Kashyapa (T4/T5) is anchored to the PLACE (built it, died at its foot) so his name is a place-fact, not a bare-name answer. Distractors = other rock forts, other fresco sites, other ancient gardens, all real. Keep answers to the rock, gate, frescoes, wall, and gardens.
history_overlap: Kashyapa's usurpation and civil war are history episodes; keep the rungs place-anchored (he BUILT the fortress and died at its base) rather than a throne-politics narrative.

name: Ellora Kailasa Temple
scope: The most astonishing rock-cut monument on Earth, at Ellora in India. T2: this full-size, multi-storey Hindu temple was not built up from blocks -- it was CARVED DOWNWARD out of one solid cliff, from the top first (answer = carved top-down from a single rock). T2/T3: to free the temple, workers chiselled away and hauled out an estimated 200,000 tonnes of rock -- and there is no way to add a piece back or fix a slip (answer = ~200,000 tonnes removed / it is a single monolith). T3: it is designed as a stone model of the Himalayan peak that Hindus believe is the god Shiva's home (answer = Mount Kailash). T3: it is Cave 16, the masterpiece, in a line of 34 rock-cut caves, raised by an 8th-century Rashtrakuta king (answer = Cave 16 / King Krishna I). T4: the same Ellora cliff holds Buddhist, Hindu AND Jain cave temples side by side, cut as those faiths shared the region (answer = three religions in one cliff). T4: the temple's outer wall carves the demon-king Ravana trapped SHAKING Mount Kailash while Shiva pins the mountain with one toe (answer = Ravana shaking Kailash). T5: full-size stone elephants, courtyards, galleries and a gateway were all left standing from the living rock as the quarry was cut away around them -- nothing was assembled (answer = it is all one continuous stone).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kailasa_Temple,_Ellora (carved top-down from a single monolith, ~200,000 tonnes of rock removed, Rashtrakuta king Krishna I 8th c, Cave 16, dedicated to Shiva / modeled on Mount Kailash, 32.6 m tall); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellora_Caves (34 rock-cut caves; Buddhist, Hindu and Jain).
framing_note: Place ladder; the carved-downward-from-one-rock, no-undo fact is the controlling wonder and dinner-test payoff -- lead with it. Accuracy rail: it is a SUBTRACTIVE monolith (200,000 tonnes removed), NOT stacked blocks -- keep that precise. Teach 'rock-cut' before leaning on it. Distractors = Ajanta, Petra, other monoliths, other Shiva sites, all real. Respect it as a living Hindu temple, not a mere feat.
history_overlap: Krishna I and Rashtrakuta dynastic history belong to history; keep answers to the carving method, scale, iconography, and the three-faith cliff.

name: Ajanta Caves
scope: A horseshoe of caves cut into a river-gorge cliff in India, hiding the finest ancient paintings in Asia. T2: some 30 Buddhist halls and monasteries were carved into the curving cliff above a bend of the Waghora river (answer = 30 rock-cut caves). T3: on their walls survive the largest body of ancient Indian PAINTING -- glowing frescoes of the Buddha's past lives (answer = the Ajanta frescoes / Jataka tales). T3: the most famous single figure is a gentle, downcast-eyed prince holding a blue lotus (answer = the Bodhisattva Padmapani). T4: after the site fell silent, jungle hid it for over a thousand years -- until 1819, when a British officer chasing a TIGER stumbled onto a cave mouth (answer = rediscovered on a tiger hunt, 1819). T4/T5: the caves come in two kinds -- living-quarters for monks, and pillared worship-halls built around a stupa (answer = viharas and chaitya halls). T5: they were cut in two bursts centuries apart, the finest work under the 5th-century Vakataka emperor Harishena before being abruptly abandoned (answer = two phases / the 460-480 CE Vakataka phase).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves (30 rock-cut Buddhist caves above the Waghora, phases ~2nd c BCE and 460-480 CE under Vakataka emperor Harishena, Jataka-tale wall paintings, Bodhisattva Padmapani, rediscovered 1819 by British officer John Smith on a tiger hunt, viharas + chaitya-grihas).
framing_note: Place ladder; the tiger-hunt rediscovery (T4) is the dinner-test payoff, the Padmapani fresco the signature image. Scene-led. Distractors = Ellora, other painted caves (Sigiriya, Dunhuang), other bodhisattvas, all real. Keep answers to the caves and their art, not the general history of Buddhism.
history_overlap: Harishena and Vakataka dynastic history belong to history; the 1819 rediscovery is a place-fact (surface it here), but keep it about the SITE, not colonial administration.

name: Taj Mahal
scope: A tomb of white marble on the Yamuna river at Agra -- grief turned into the most beautiful building in the world. T1: Emperor Shah Jahan raised it not as a palace but as a TOMB for one person he had lost (answer = his wife Mumtaz Mahal). T2: the whole thing is skinned in white marble hauled ~400 km from a single quarry town in Rajasthan (answer = Makrana marble). T2/T3: that marble seems to change color through the day -- pink at dawn, white by noon, gold under the moon (answer = it shifts color with the light). T3: its four minarets are built leaning slightly OUTWARD on purpose, so that in an earthquake they would topple away from the tomb, not onto it (answer = tilted outward for earthquake safety). T4: the flowers on its walls aren't painted -- they're pictures inlaid from thousands of cut gemstones set flush into the marble (answer = pietra dura / stone inlay). T4: it took some 20,000 workers and artisans over 20 years, drawing masters from Persia and beyond (answer = ~22 years / ~20,000 artisans). T5: the tale that Shah Jahan planned a matching BLACK Taj across the river for himself is a romantic myth -- the 'black' ruins were white marble darkened by age (answer = the Black Taj is a legend).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taj_Mahal (Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal, commissioned 1631 / built 1632-1653, Makrana white marble, color-shift under changing light, minarets tilted outward for quake safety, pietra dura inlay, >20,000 artisans / ~22 years, Black Taj legend debunked as darkened white marble).
framing_note: Place ladder; the tilted-minarets earthquake trick (T3) and the pietra dura (T4) are the dinner-test payoffs, the grief origin the T1 hook. Accuracy rail: explicitly flag the Black Taj as legend/myth (T5). Distractors = other Mughal tombs (Humayun's), other marble/inlay facts, all real. Respect it as a real tomb, not a photo-op. CROSS-LISTED with history -- see history_overlap.
history_overlap: CROSS-LISTED with history: Shah Jahan's reign, his deposition and imprisonment by his son Aurangzeb, and Mughal succession are history episodes -- geography keeps ONLY the place-wonders (marble source, color-shift, tilted minarets, pietra dura, Black Taj myth). If history also builds Shah Jahan, coordinate so the tomb-as-architecture facts live HERE and the dynasty facts live THERE.

name: Mohenjo-daro & the Indus Cities
scope: One of the world's first great cities, built ~2500 BCE on the Indus -- and one of its deepest mysteries. T1: 4,500 years ago its streets were laid in a neat GRID of right angles, like a planned modern city, long before Greece or Rome (answer = a planned grid of streets). T2: nearly every house connected to covered brick DRAINS running under the streets -- the world's oldest citywide sewage system (answer = covered street drains / sewers). T3: at its heart sits a great watertight brick POOL, sealed with tar, that may be the world's oldest ritual bath (answer = the Great Bath). T3: we can read Egyptian and Sumerian writing, but the Indus people's SCRIPT has never been cracked -- thousands of tiny inscribed seals stay silent (answer = the undeciphered Indus script). T4: we don't even know what the city called itself -- its modern name just means 'Mound of the Dead' in the local tongue (answer = its true name is unknown). T4: unlike Egypt it left no giant royal tombs, no obvious king's palace or temple -- hinting at a strangely equal society (answer = no kings' palaces or tombs found). T4: two objects star from the ruins -- a poised soapstone 'Priest-King' and a tiny, confident bronze 'Dancing Girl' (answer = the Dancing Girl / Priest-King). T5: at the sister-city of Lothal, archaeologists found what may be the world's oldest DOCK, a brick basin linked to the sea (answer = the Lothal dockyard). T5: after centuries the Indus cities were quietly abandoned -- leading theories blame a shifting, drying river and a failing monsoon, not conquest (answer = river shift / monsoon failure -- flag as leading theory).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro (~2500 BCE, grid plan, ~700 wells + citywide covered drainage 'one well per three houses', Great Bath 12x7 m sealed with bitumen, undeciphered Indus script, name = 'Mound of the Dead Men' in Sindhi, Priest-King soapstone + Dancing Girl bronze ~10.5 cm, abandonment); Lothal / Harappan sites (brick dockyard basin) from established domain knowledge.
framing_note: Place ladder; the undeciphered-script + unknown-name pair (T3/T4) is the dinner-test mystery payoff, the covered drains the 'they had sewers before Rome' hook. Accuracy rail: label the abandonment as leading THEORY (river shift / monsoon), not settled fact, and the 'egalitarian, no kings' reading as an interpretation. Distractors = Egypt, Sumer/Ur, other early cities, other Indus sites (Harappa, Dholavira, Lothal), all real. LANE: the Dancing Girl / Priest-King are ARTIFACTS of the place (fine as place-facts); the monsoon-failure rung ties to the climate theme but keeps the answer the site's fate.
history_overlap: The Indus Civilization's broad rise-and-fall as a chapter of world history overlaps history; geography keeps the URBAN wonders (grid, drains, Great Bath, script, artifacts, dockyard). A pure 'what caused the collapse' debate with no site anchor belongs to history.

name: The Great Wall of China
scope: Not one wall but a 2,000-year system of walls snaking across northern China's mountains and deserts. T1: add up every branch and the walls run an almost unbelievable distance -- over 21,000 km, roughly half the Earth's circumference (invert the wonder: the huge number is the hook; answer = ~21,000 km / 21,196 km). T2: the popular claim that you can see it from the Moon with the naked eye is FALSE -- from orbit it's thinner than a human hair viewed from 3 km away (answer = the 'visible from space' myth is false). T2/T3: it isn't a single wall from one reign -- it's many walls built and rebuilt over ~2,000 years by different dynasties (answer = many walls over many dynasties). T3: the grand stone-and-brick wall most tourists picture is mostly the work of ONE dynasty, about 8,850 km of it (answer = the Ming wall). T3: out in the western deserts, older stretches were built not of brick but of rammed earth and layered reeds -- and still stand (answer = rammed / tamped-earth wall). T4: the wall's real job wasn't a magic barrier but a control-and-communication line -- beacon towers relaying smoke-and-fire signals faster than a horse could gallop (answer = the beacon-tower signal relay). T4: the eastern end plunges into the sea at a fort nicknamed the 'Old Dragon's Head' (answer = Shanhaiguan / Old Dragon's Head). T5: the grim legend that dead laborers were buried IN the wall is largely a myth -- but the human cost of building it, over centuries of forced labor, was staggeringly real (answer = the 'bones in the wall' is legend, the death toll real).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China (2012 comprehensive survey 21,196.18 km total, Ming wall ~8,850 km, built Qin through Qing across many dynasties, 'visible from Moon with naked eye' debunked, beacon-tower signalling, rammed-earth western sections, eastern terminus at Shanhaiguan 'Old Dragon's Head').
framing_note: Place ladder; the 'from space' myth-bust (T2) and the 21,000-km hook (T1) are the dinner-test payoffs. Invert the wonder -- lead with the huge number, make the myth-bust the knowable answer. Accuracy rail: it's a SYSTEM of walls, not one; label 'bones in the wall' as legend while stating the real forced-labor human cost plainly (honest both ways). Distractors = other great walls (Hadrian's), other superlatives, all real. Keep answers to the wall/place, not the dynastic wars it defended against.
history_overlap: The wars, dynasties, and the nomad-vs-China conflict the wall was built for belong to history; geography keeps the wall's length, construction, materials, signal system, and endpoints. State the forced-labor human cost as fact, but the campaigns are history.

name: The Terracotta Army
scope: An underground army of life-size clay soldiers guarding the tomb of China's First Emperor near Mount Li. T2: in 1974, farmers digging a WELL broke into a buried pit and hit the head of a clay soldier -- then found thousands more (answer = discovered by well-digging farmers, 1974). T2/T3: more than 8,000 life-size warriors stand in battle order in the pits, plus hundreds of horses and chariots (answer = ~8,000 soldiers). T3: no two faces are the same -- each soldier was given individual features, so the army looks like a crowd of real, distinct men (answer = every face is unique). T4: the ancient historian Sima Qian wrote that the emperor's tomb held a map of the empire with a hundred RIVERS OF LIQUID MERCURY, made to flow mechanically (answer = rivers of mercury). T4: astonishingly, soil tests over the still-sealed tomb mound show unnaturally HIGH mercury levels -- matching the 2,000-year-old account (answer = high mercury detected in the mound). T5: the emperor's actual burial chamber has never been opened -- archaeologists deliberately leave it sealed rather than risk destroying what's inside (answer = the tomb is still unexcavated). T5: the whole army faces EAST, toward the lands the First Emperor had conquered, set to guard him forever (answer = they face east, toward the conquered lands).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army (discovered March 1974 by well-digging farmers near Mount Li, >8,000 soldiers + 130 chariots / 520+150 horses, individualized faces from base forms, Sima Qian's account of mercury rivers corroborated by high mercury in the tomb-mound soil, central burial chamber unexcavated).
framing_note: Place ladder; the mercury-rivers-confirmed-by-soil-tests (T4) and the never-opened tomb (T5) are the dinner-test payoffs. Scene-led -- open with the well-diggers' shock, not a definition. Accuracy rail: keep the mercury as Sima Qian's account CORROBORATED by real soil readings, and don't overclaim the tomb's unseen contents; AVOID the disputed 'chrome-plated swords' claim. Distractors = other tombs (Egyptian pyramids), other grave-goods, all real.
history_overlap: Qin Shi Huang unifying China, standardizing script and measures, Legalism, and the book-burnings are history episodes; geography keeps the TOMB-complex wonders (the pits, the army, the mercury, the sealed chamber, the eastward facing).

name: Leshan Giant Buddha
scope: The largest pre-modern stone Buddha on Earth, carved into a cliff where three rivers meet in China. T2: a monk began carving this Buddha in 713 CE hoping the huge holy figure would CALM the deadly rapids that were wrecking boats at the river junction (answer = to calm the turbulent waters). T3: it is colossal -- 71 m tall, so big that a grown person is dwarfed by its EAR alone and can stand on a single toenail (answer = 71 metres / the world's largest stone Buddha). T3: it sits at the meeting of three rivers, gazing across the water at a sacred mountain (answer = the confluence of the Min, Dadu and Qingyi). T4: hidden inside the statue is an ingenious DRAINAGE system -- channels cut through its hair, collar and body carry rainwater away so it doesn't erode (answer = a hidden drainage system). T4/T5: whether or not it calmed the river spiritually, cutting it dumped so much rock into the water that the currents really were tamed (answer = the discarded rock actually calmed the currents). T5: it took ~90 years and three generations to finish, stalling when the monk's funds ran out and resuming under later patrons (answer = ~90 years, 713-803).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leshan_Giant_Buddha (71 m, largest/tallest pre-modern stone Buddha, monk Hai Tong began 713 CE to calm turbulent waters, confluence of Min/Dadu/Qingyi facing Mount Emei, hidden internal drainage channels, ~90 years to completion ~803 CE).

Distractors = other giant Buddhas (Bamiyan), other river/mountain sites, all real. Respect it as a sacred image.

name: Konark Sun Temple
scope: A 13th-century temple on India's Odisha coast, built as a colossal stone chariot for the sun god. T2: the entire temple is shaped as the war-chariot of Surya the sun god -- a giant vehicle carved in stone (answer = a chariot of the sun god / Surya). T3: that chariot rides on 24 huge, richly carved stone WHEELS and is pulled by seven straining stone horses (answer = 24 wheels and 7 horses). T3: the wheels aren't just decoration -- their spokes and hub work as SUNDIALS, casting shadows that tell the time of day (answer = the wheels are working sundials). T4: European sailors used it as a navigation landmark and called it the 'Black Pagoda,' opposite the 'White Pagoda' up the coast (answer = the Black Pagoda). T4/T5: its towering main spire has COLLAPSED -- only the great audience hall still stands, and legend blames a lodestone at the top that once wrecked ships' compasses (answer = the main tower collapsed / lodestone legend).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konark_Sun_Temple (~1250 CE, King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, giant stone chariot of Surya with 24 carved wheels + 7 horses, wheels function as sundials, main shikhara collapsed / ~39 m jagamohana survives, 'Black Pagoda' sailors' landmark on the Odisha / Bay of Bengal coast).
framing_note: Place ladder; the wheels-that-tell-time (T3) is the dinner-test payoff, the whole-temple-is-a-chariot the controlling image. Scene-led. Accuracy rail: the sundial function is real; the ship-wrecking 'lodestone at the summit' is legend -- flag it as such. Distractors = other Surya/sun temples, other chariot iconography, other coastal landmarks, all real. Keep answers to the temple's form and setting.
history_overlap: Narasimhadeva I and Eastern Ganga dynastic history belong to history; keep answers to the chariot form, the wheels/sundials, the collapse, and the Black-Pagoda landmark.
